notes:
1. Meaning of Judiciary

The Judiciary is one of the three organs of Government along with:

  • Legislature.
  • Executive.

It consists of courts established to:

  • Interpret laws.
  • Administer justice.
  • Resolve disputes.
  • Protect constitutional rights.

2. Constitutional Role

The Judiciary performs functions such as:

  • Interpreting the Constitution.
  • Protecting Fundamental Rights.
  • Settling disputes.
  • Upholding Rule of Law.
  • Safeguarding constitutional supremacy.
  • Reviewing unconstitutional Government action.

3. Disputes Decided by Judiciary

Courts may resolve disputes between:

  • Individuals.
  • Individuals and Government.
  • State Governments.
  • Union and States.
  • Constitutional authorities.

4. Integrated Judicial System

India follows:

  • A Single Integrated Judicial System.

Unlike federations with separate federal and State court systems, India possesses:

  • One unified judicial hierarchy.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → Single Integrated Judiciary

5. Judicial Hierarchy

The broad hierarchy is:

  • Supreme Court.
  • High Courts.
  • District and Sessions Courts.
  • Subordinate Courts.

6. Supreme Court at the Apex

Supreme Court of India is:

  • Highest judicial authority.
  • Apex Court.
  • Final Court of Appeal.

7. High Courts

  • High Courts are the highest constitutional courts at the State level.

A High Court may serve:

  • One State.
  • More than one State or Union Territory under constitutional arrangements.

8. District and Sessions Courts

At district level:

  • Civil jurisdiction is generally exercised by District Courts.
  • Criminal jurisdiction is generally exercised by Sessions Courts.

9. Subordinate Courts

Subordinate Courts may include:

  • Civil Courts.
  • Criminal Courts.
  • Family Courts.
  • Other courts established under law.

10. Independent Judiciary

Judicial independence is protected through safeguards such as:

  • Security of tenure.
  • Protected removal procedure.
  • Fixed service conditions.
  • Financial safeguards.
  • Separation from Executive in judicial functions.
  • Constitutional status.

11. Importance of Judicial Independence

Judicial independence:

  • Protects democracy.
  • Prevents abuse of power.
  • Protects rights.
  • Ensures impartial justice.
  • Maintains constitutional government.
  • Builds public confidence.

12. Guardian of Constitution

The Judiciary safeguards:

  • Supremacy of Constitution.
  • Fundamental Rights.
  • Constitutional values.
  • Limits on Government power.

13. Judicial Review

Judicial Review allows courts to examine whether:

  • Laws.
  • Executive actions.
  • Constitutional amendments within Basic Structure limits

conform to the Constitution.

📌 Must-Memorise

Judicial Review → Constitutional Validity of Laws and Executive Action

14. Rule of Law

The Judiciary ensures:

  • No person is above law.

Public authorities act according to:

  • Constitution.
  • Law.

15. Protector of Fundamental Rights

Supreme Court and High Courts protect Fundamental Rights through:

  • Constitutional remedies.
  • Writ jurisdiction.

16. Article 32

Article 32 empowers Supreme Court to issue writs for:

  • Enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described Article 32 as:

  • “Heart and Soul of the Constitution.”
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 32 → Supreme Court Writs → Fundamental Rights

17. Article 226

Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs:

  • For Fundamental Rights.
  • For any other purpose.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 226 → Wider Writ Jurisdiction than Article 32

18. Five Constitutional Writs

The source lists:

  • Habeas Corpus.
  • Mandamus.
  • Prohibition.
  • Certiorari.
  • Quo Warranto.

19. Court of Record

Both:

  • Supreme Court.
  • High Courts

are Courts of Record.

20. Article 129

Article 129 declares Supreme Court:

  • Court of Record.

It has power to punish for:

  • Contempt of Court.

21. Article 215

Article 215 declares every High Court:

  • Court of Record.

High Courts may punish for:

  • Contempt of Court.

22. Article 141

Law declared by Supreme Court is binding on:

  • All courts within India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 141 → Supreme Court Law Binding on All Courts

23. Judicial Precedent

Judicial precedent promotes:

  • Uniformity.
  • Consistency.
  • Certainty

in interpretation and application of law.

24. Open Court System

Court proceedings are generally:

  • Open to public.

This supports:

  • Transparency.
  • Fairness.
  • Public confidence.

Certain proceedings may be held:

  • In camera

where law permits.

25. Article 50

Article 50 directs the State to separate:

  • Judiciary

from:

  • Executive

in public services of the State.

📌 Must-Memorise

Article 50 → Separation of Judiciary from Executive

26. Article 50 Classification

Article 50 is a:

  • Directive Principle of State Policy.

27. Constitutional Provisions

Supreme Court is dealt with in:

  • Part V.
  • Chapter IV.
  • Articles 124–147.
📌 Must-Memorise

Supreme Court → Articles 124–147

28. Establishment of Supreme Court

The Supreme Court came into existence on:

  • 28 January 1950.
📌 Must-Memorise

Supreme Court → 28 January 1950

29. Institutions Replaced

The Supreme Court replaced the apex role previously associated with:

  • Federal Court of India.
  • Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.

30. Article 124

Article 124 deals with:

  • Establishment of Supreme Court.
  • Appointment of Judges.
  • Qualifications.
  • Conditions of office.
  • Removal.

31. Composition

Supreme Court consists of:

  • Chief Justice of India.
  • Such number of other Judges as Parliament may prescribe by law.

32. Appointment of Supreme Court Judges

Supreme Court Judges are appointed by:

  • President of India.

33. Chief Justice of India

By constitutional convention:

Senior-most Supreme Court Judge is ordinarily appointed as:

  • Chief Justice of India.

Formal appointment is made by:

  • President.

34. Qualification — Citizenship

A Supreme Court Judge must be:

  • Citizen of India.

35. Qualification — High Court Judge

A person qualifies if he or she has been:

  • Judge of a High Court.
  • Or of two or more High Courts in succession

for at least:

  • Five years.

36. Qualification — Advocate

A person also qualifies if he or she has been:

  • Advocate of a High Court.
  • Or two or more High Courts in succession

for at least:

  • Ten years.

37. Distinguished Jurist

A person may also qualify if:

  • In opinion of President,

he or she is a:

  • Distinguished Jurist.
📌 Must-Memorise

SC Judge → HC Judge 5 Years / HC Advocate 10 Years / Distinguished Jurist

38. Oath of Supreme Court Judge

Oath or affirmation is made before:

  • President.
  • Or person appointed by President.

39. Supreme Court Retirement Age

A Supreme Court Judge holds office until:

  • 65 years.
📌 Must-Memorise

Supreme Court Judge → Retirement Age 65

40. Resignation of Supreme Court Judge

A Supreme Court Judge resigns by writing to:

  • President.

41. Grounds for Removal

A Supreme Court Judge may be removed for:

  • Proved Misbehaviour.
  • Incapacity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Judge Removal → Proved Misbehaviour or Incapacity

42. Removal Majority

Removal requires an address by each House of Parliament supported by:

  • Majority of total membership.
  • Not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.

43. Formal Removal

After the Parliamentary address:

  • President removes the Judge.

44. Article 125

Article 125 deals with:

  • Salaries and allowances of Supreme Court Judges.
  • They are determined by Parliament.

Salaries are charged on:

  • Consolidated Fund of India.

45. Service-Condition Protection

Supreme Court Judges' service conditions cannot ordinarily be varied:

  • To their disadvantage after appointment,

except as constitutionally permitted during:

  • Financial Emergency.

46. Article 126

Article 126 deals with:

  • Acting Chief Justice of India.

47. Appointment of Acting CJI

President may appoint a Supreme Court Judge as Acting CJI when:

  • CJI office is vacant.
  • CJI is unable to perform duties.

48. Article 127

Article 127 deals with:

  • Ad Hoc Judges of Supreme Court.

49. Ad Hoc Judge

If sufficient quorum is unavailable:

  • CJI may request a qualified High Court Judge to sit as an Ad Hoc Judge.

Previous consent of:

  • President

is required.

50. Article 128

Article 128 deals with:

  • Attendance of retired Judges at sittings of Supreme Court.

51. Retired Judge Sitting in Supreme Court

CJI may request:

  • Retired Supreme Court Judge.
  • Qualified retired High Court Judge

to sit and act as Supreme Court Judge subject to:

  • Prescribed conditions.
  • Consent of concerned Judge.

52. Article 130

Seat of Supreme Court is:

  • New Delhi.

Supreme Court may sit elsewhere if:

  • CJI so decides.
  • President approves.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 130 → Seat of Supreme Court → New Delhi

53. Post-Retirement Restriction

A retired Supreme Court Judge:

  • Cannot plead or act in any court.
  • Cannot plead or act before any authority within India.

54. Types of Jurisdiction

The source lists:

  • Original.
  • Writ.
  • Appellate.
  • Advisory.
  • Review.
  • Curative.
  • Court of Record jurisdiction.

55. Article 131

Article 131 provides:

  • Exclusive Original Jurisdiction of Supreme Court.

56. Original Jurisdiction Disputes

It covers disputes involving:

  • Union and one or more States.
  • Union and State(s) on one side versus other State(s).
  • Two or more States.

57. Legal Right Requirement

For Article 131 jurisdiction:

  • Dispute must involve a question of law or fact upon which existence or extent of a legal right depends.

58. Article 132

Article 132 deals with appeals involving:

  • Substantial questions of constitutional interpretation.

59. Article 133

Article 133 deals with:

  • Civil appeals from High Courts.

60. Article 134

Article 134 deals with:

  • Criminal appeals.

61. Article 136

Article 136 empowers Supreme Court to grant:

  • Special Leave to Appeal.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 136 → Special Leave Petition

62. Nature of SLP

Special Leave is:

  • Extraordinary.
  • Discretionary.

It may arise from judgments or orders of courts and tribunals, subject to constitutional exclusions.

63. Armed Forces Exception

The source notes that Article 136 excludes specified matters relating to:

  • Armed Forces tribunals/courts

within the constitutional limitation stated.

64. Article 137

Article 137 empowers Supreme Court to:

  • Review its own judgments.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 137 → Review Jurisdiction

65. Curative Petition

Curative Petition:

  • Is judicially evolved.
  • May be entertained in exceptional situations after dismissal of review petition.
  • Seeks to prevent miscarriage of justice.

66. Article 143

Article 143 provides:

  • Advisory Jurisdiction of Supreme Court.

67. Presidential Reference

President may refer:

  • Questions of law.
  • Matters of public importance

to Supreme Court for its opinion.

68. Nature of Advisory Opinion

The source describes the Supreme Court's Article 143 opinion as:

  • Advisory in nature.

69. Article 142

Article 142 empowers Supreme Court to pass orders necessary for:

  • Complete Justice

in matters pending before it.

📌 Must-Memorise

Article 142 → Complete Justice

70. Article 144

Article 144 requires:

  • Civil authorities.
  • Judicial authorities

to act in aid of:

  • Supreme Court.

71. Article 145

Article 145 deals with:

  • Rules of Supreme Court.
  • Practice.
  • Procedure.

72. Article 146

Article 146 deals with:

  • Officers.
  • Servants.
  • Administrative expenses

of Supreme Court.

73. Article 147

Article 147 provides interpretation of specified expressions used in:

  • Part V, Chapter IV.

74. Constitutional Provisions

High Courts are principally covered under:

  • Articles 214–231.
📌 Must-Memorise

High Courts → Articles 214–231

75. Article 214

Article 214 provides:

  • A High Court for each State.

76. Common High Court

The constitutional framework permits:

  • A common High Court for two or more States or Union Territories.

77. Article 217

Article 217 deals with:

  • Appointment.
  • Qualifications.
  • Conditions of office

of High Court Judges.

78. Appointment of High Court Judges

High Court Judges are appointed by:

  • President of India.

79. High Court Retirement Age

High Court Judge retires at:

  • 62 years.
📌 Must-Memorise

SC Judge → 65 HC Judge → 62

80. Article 222

Article 222 deals with:

  • Transfer of High Court Judges.

Transfer is made by:

  • President

after consultation with:

  • Chief Justice of India.

81. Article 227

Article 227 gives every High Court:

  • Superintendence over courts and tribunals within its territorial jurisdiction

subject to constitutional and legal exceptions.

📌 Must-Memorise

Article 227 → High Court Superintendence

82. Supreme Court vs High Court Writs

Supreme Court:

  • Article 32.
  • Fundamental Rights.

High Court:

  • Article 226.
  • Fundamental Rights.
  • Other legal rights.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Article 226 → Wider Scope than Article 32

83. Article 233

Article 233 deals with:

  • Appointment of District Judges.

84. Appointment of District Judges

District Judges are appointed by:

  • Governor

in consultation with:

  • High Court.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 233 → Governor + High Court Consultation

85. Article 235

Article 235 vests control over:

  • District Courts.
  • Subordinate Courts

in:

  • High Court.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 235 → High Court Control over Subordinate Courts

86. Importance of High Court Control

Article 235 strengthens:

  • Judicial independence.
  • Administrative control of Judiciary.
  • Separation from Executive.

87. Constitutional Basis of Judicial Review

The source identifies provisions including:

  • Article 13.
  • Article 32.
  • Article 131.
  • Article 136.
  • Article 226.
  • Article 227.

88. Judicial Review as Basic Structure

The Supreme Court has recognised:

  • Judicial Review

as part of:

  • Basic Structure of Constitution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Judicial Review → Basic Structure

89. Objectives of Judicial Review

Judicial Review seeks to:

  • Protect Constitution.
  • Safeguard Fundamental Rights.
  • Prevent abuse of power.
  • Maintain constitutional supremacy.
  • Ensure legality of Government action.

90. Judicial Activism

Judicial Activism refers to an approach where courts actively interpret Constitution and laws to promote:

  • Justice.
  • Public welfare.
  • Fundamental Rights.
  • Good governance.

91. Areas of Judicial Activism

The source mentions:

  • Environmental protection.
  • Prison reforms.
  • Gender justice.
  • Electoral transparency.
  • Fundamental Rights.

92. Judicial Restraint

Judicial Restraint means courts should:

  • Exercise powers cautiously.
  • Avoid unnecessary interference in Legislature and Executive functions.
  • Intervene where constitutional or legal violation requires judicial action.

93. Importance of Judicial Restraint

It helps maintain:

  • Separation of Powers.
  • Respect for democratic institutions.
  • Institutional balance.
  • Limits on judicial overreach.

94. Judicial Activism vs Restraint

Judicial Activism:

  • Broader interpretation.
  • Greater intervention where constitutionally justified.

Judicial Restraint:

  • Limited intervention.
  • Greater institutional deference.

95. Meaning of PIL

Public Interest Litigation allows a person or organisation to approach court for protection of:

  • Public interest.
  • Fundamental Rights.
  • Rights of disadvantaged groups.

96. Relaxed Locus Standi

In PIL:

  • Petitioner need not always be personally affected by the issue.
  • Public-spirited persons may approach constitutional courts for public causes.

97. Origin of PIL

The source states that PIL developed through Supreme Court decisions during:

  • Late 1970s.
  • 1980s.

98. PIL Constitutional Basis

PIL is generally filed under:

  • Article 32 → Supreme Court.
  • Article 226 → High Courts.

99. Common PIL Areas

The source identifies:

  • Environment.
  • Human rights.
  • Prison reforms.
  • Child rights.
  • Women's rights.
  • Consumer welfare.
  • Electoral transparency.
  • Public health.
  • Government accountability.

100. Importance of PIL

PIL has:

  • Expanded access to justice.
  • Protected disadvantaged groups.
  • Strengthened Government accountability.
  • Increased public participation in constitutional justice.

101. Meaning of Contempt

Contempt of Court refers to acts that:

  • Obstruct administration of justice.
  • Lower authority of courts.
  • Wilfully disobey lawful court orders.

102. Statutory Framework

The source refers to:

  • Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.

103. Civil Contempt

Civil Contempt generally includes:

Wilful disobedience of:

  • Judgment.
  • Decree.
  • Direction.
  • Order.
  • Writ.
  • Court process.
  • Wilful breach of an undertaking given to court.

104. Criminal Contempt

Criminal Contempt generally includes acts that:

  • Scandalise or tend to scandalise court authority.
  • Prejudice judicial proceedings.
  • Interfere with judicial proceedings.
  • Obstruct administration of justice.

105. Purpose of Contempt Power

Contempt jurisdiction protects:

  • Judicial authority.
  • Compliance with court orders.
  • Effective administration of justice.
  • Public confidence.

106. Gram Nyayalayas Act

Gram Nyayalayas were established under:

  • Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gram Nyayalayas → Act of 2008

107. Purpose of Gram Nyayalayas

They seek to:

  • Provide inexpensive justice.
  • Deliver speedy justice.
  • Bring courts closer to rural people.
  • Reduce burden on regular courts.

108. Jurisdiction of Gram Nyayalayas

They deal with specified:

  • Civil matters.
  • Criminal matters

as provided under law.

109. Meaning of Collegium

The Collegium System governs recommendations for appointment and transfer of Judges of:

  • Supreme Court.
  • High Courts.

110. Constitutional Position of Collegium

Collegium System is:

  • Judicially evolved.
  • It is not expressly mentioned in the Constitution.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Collegium → Judicial Creation, Not Expressly in Constitution

111. Judges Cases

The Collegium evolved through:

  • First Judges Case, 1981.
  • Second Judges Case, 1993.
  • Third Judges Case, 1998.

112. First Judges Case

S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, 1981:

  • Gave greater importance to Executive role in judicial appointments.
  • Consultation was not treated as concurrence under the interpretation adopted in that case.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Judges Case → 1981 → Executive Primacy

113. Second Judges Case

Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India, 1993:

  • Established Collegium System.
  • Recognised judicial primacy in higher judicial appointments.
📌 Must-Memorise

Second Judges Case → 1993 → Collegium Established

114. Third Judges Case

Re Presidential Reference, 1998:

Clarified:

  • Collegium composition.
  • Appointment procedure.
  • Consultation process.
📌 Must-Memorise

Third Judges Case → 1998 → Collegium Clarified

115. Supreme Court Collegium Composition

The source states that Supreme Court Collegium consists of:

  • Chief Justice of India.
  • Four senior-most Supreme Court Judges.

116. High Court Appointment Process

For High Court appointments:

Recommendation ordinarily originates from:

  • Chief Justice of concerned High Court.

It is considered by:

  • Supreme Court Collegium.

Appointment is ultimately made by:

  • President.

117. Reiterated Collegium Recommendation

The source states that if Collegium reiterates a recommendation after reconsideration:

  • It is ordinarily binding under prevailing constitutional framework.

118. Criticism of Collegium

Criticisms include:

  • Lack of transparency.
  • Absence of formal selection criteria.
  • Limited accountability.
  • Closed decision-making.
  • Lack of written reasons in many cases.

119. Ninety-Ninth Constitutional Amendment

The 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014 sought to establish:

  • National Judicial Appointments Commission.

120. NJAC Act

Parliament also enacted:

  • National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014.

121. Objective of NJAC

NJAC sought to replace:

  • Collegium System

with a body involving:

  • Judiciary.
  • Executive.
  • Eminent persons.

122. NJAC Composition

The proposed NJAC consisted of:

  • Chief Justice of India — Chairperson.
  • Two senior-most Supreme Court Judges.
  • Union Minister for Law and Justice.
  • Two eminent persons.
📌 Must-Memorise

NJAC → CJI + 2 SC Judges + Law Minister + 2 Eminent Persons

123. NJAC Functions

NJAC was intended to recommend:

  • Supreme Court appointments.
  • High Court appointments.
  • High Court Judge transfers.

124. Fourth Judges Case, 2015

Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India, 2015:

Struck down:

  • 99th Constitutional Amendment.
  • NJAC Act, 2014.

Restored:

  • Collegium System.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fourth Judges Case → 2015 → NJAC Struck Down

125. Principle in NJAC Case

The Supreme Court held:

Judicial Independence forms part of:

  • Basic Structure.

126. Collegium vs NJAC

Collegium:

  • Judicially evolved.
  • Judicial primacy.
  • Currently operates.

NJAC:

  • Created by 99th Amendment and NJAC Act.
  • Included Executive and eminent persons.
  • Declared unconstitutional in 2015.

127. Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment, 1976

The attachment associates the 42nd Amendment with:

  • Curtailment of certain Judicial Review powers.
  • Restrictions on some High Court jurisdiction.
  • Tribunal-related provisions.
  • Greater Parliamentary authority during Emergency period.
📌 Must-Memorise

42nd Amendment → Attempted Curtailment of Judicial Powers

128. Forty-Third Constitutional Amendment, 1977

The 43rd Amendment:

  • Restored several judicial powers curtailed by 42nd Amendment.

Strengthened:

  • Judicial Review.
  • Constitutional balance.
📌 Must-Memorise

43rd Amendment → Restoration of Judicial Powers

129. Forty-Fourth Constitutional Amendment, 1978

The attachment associates the 44th Amendment with:

  • Restoring democratic safeguards.
  • Strengthening civil liberties.
  • Reinforcing Judiciary's constitutional role after Emergency.

130. Ninety-Ninth Constitutional Amendment, 2014

  • Established NJAC framework.

Later declared unconstitutional by Supreme Court in:

  • 2015.

131. One Hundred and Third Constitutional Amendment, 2019

Introduced:

  • 10% EWS reservation.
  • Constitutional validity was challenged before Supreme Court.

132. Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India, 2022

The source states that Supreme Court:

  • Upheld constitutional validity of 103rd Amendment.
  • Demonstrated continuing judicial review of constitutional amendments under Basic Structure framework.

133. Golaknath v. State of Punjab, 1967

The Supreme Court held under the constitutional interpretation adopted at that time:

  • Parliament could not amend Fundamental Rights.

The position was later modified by:

  • Kesavananda Bharati.
📌 Must-Memorise

Golaknath → 1967 → Parliament's Amending Power

134. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973

The Supreme Court evolved:

  • Basic Structure Doctrine.

Kesavananda Bharati → 1973 → Basic Structure Doctrine

135. Basic Structure Principle

Parliament may amend Constitution under Article 368 but cannot:

  • Alter.
  • Destroy

its Basic Structure.

136. Basic Structure Features in Source

The attachment identifies features including:

  • Supremacy of Constitution.
  • Rule of Law.
  • Judicial Review.
  • Judicial Independence.
  • Federalism.
  • Separation of Powers.

  • Fair.

  • Right to Speedy Trial

Supreme Court framed:

  • Vishaka Guidelines

to address:

  • Sexual harassment at workplace

142. Tribunals and Judicial Review

Tribunal decisions remain subject to:

  • High Court Judicial Review.

L. Chandra Kumar → 1997 → Tribunal Decisions Reviewable by High Courts

What is the Judiciary? → Constitutional system of courts that interprets law and administers justice.

What are the three major organs of Government? → Legislature, Executive and Judiciary.

What type of judicial system does India follow? → Single Integrated Judicial System.

What is the hierarchy? → Supreme Court → High Courts → District/Sessions Courts → Subordinate Courts.

Which is the highest court? → Supreme Court of India.

Which Article directs separation of Judiciary from Executive? → Article 50.

Is Article 50 a Fundamental Right? → No.

What is it? → Directive Principle of State Policy.

Which Article makes Supreme Court law binding on all courts? → Article 141.

Which courts are Courts of Record? → Supreme Court and High Courts.

Which Article makes Supreme Court a Court of Record? → Article 129.

Which Article makes High Court a Court of Record? → Article 215.

Which Part and Articles principally govern Supreme Court? → Part V, Articles 124–147.

When did Supreme Court come into existence? → 28 January 1950.

Which institutions did it replace at the apex level? → Federal Court of India and Judicial Committee of Privy Council.

Which Article deals with Supreme Court establishment and Judges? → Article 124.

Who appoints Supreme Court Judges? → President.

Who is ordinarily appointed CJI by convention? → Senior-most Supreme Court Judge.

What citizenship qualification is required? → Indian citizenship.

How many years as High Court Judge qualify a person for Supreme Court appointment? → At least five years.

How many years as High Court Advocate? → At least ten years.

Can a distinguished jurist become Supreme Court Judge? → Yes, if President considers the person a distinguished jurist.

What is retirement age of Supreme Court Judge? → 65 years.

What is retirement age of High Court Judge? → 62 years.

To whom does Supreme Court Judge resign? → President.

What are the two grounds for removal? → Proved Misbehaviour and Incapacity.

What majority is needed in each House for removal? → Majority of total membership plus not less than two-thirds present and voting.

Who formally removes the Judge? → President.

Which Article deals with salaries of Supreme Court Judges? → Article 125.

On which Fund are salaries charged? → Consolidated Fund of India.

Which Article provides Acting CJI? → Article 126.

Which Article provides Ad Hoc Judges? → Article 127.

Whose previous consent is required for Ad Hoc Judge arrangement stated in the source? → President.

Which Article deals with retired Judges sitting in Supreme Court? → Article 128.

Which Article specifies Supreme Court's seat? → Article 130.

Where is it? → New Delhi.

Can Supreme Court sit elsewhere? → Yes, if CJI decides with President's approval.

Which Article gives Original Jurisdiction? → Article 131.

What disputes are covered? → Union–State and inter-State disputes involving legal rights.

Which Article deals with constitutional appeals? → Article 132.

Civil appeals? → Article 133.

Criminal appeals? → Article 134.

Which Article gives Special Leave jurisdiction? → Article 136.

What does SLP stand for? → Special Leave Petition.

Is Article 136 discretionary? → Yes.

Which Article allows Supreme Court to review its judgment? → Article 137.

What is a Curative Petition? → Exceptional judicially evolved remedy after review dismissal to prevent miscarriage of justice.

Which Article gives advisory jurisdiction? → Article 143.

Who seeks the advisory opinion? → President.

What may be referred? → Questions of law or public importance.

Which Article gives Complete Justice power? → Article 142.

Which Article requires civil and judicial authorities to aid Supreme Court? → Article 144.

Which Article gives Supreme Court rule-making power? → Article 145.

Which Article concerns SC officers and servants? → Article 146.

Which Article deals with High Court for each State? → Article 214.

Can two States share a High Court? → Yes.

Which Article deals with appointment of High Court Judges? → Article 217.

Who appoints High Court Judges? → President.

Which Article permits transfer of High Court Judges? → Article 222.

Who transfers them? → President after consultation with CJI.

Which Article gives High Courts Writ Jurisdiction? → Article 226.

Why is Article 226 wider than Article 32? → It covers Fundamental Rights and other legal rights.

Which Article gives High Court superintendence? → Article 227.

Which Article deals with District Judge appointments? → Article 233.

Who appoints District Judges? → Governor in consultation with High Court.

Which Article gives control over subordinate courts to High Court? → Article 235.

What is Judicial Review? → Court examination of constitutional validity of laws and executive actions.

Is Judicial Review part of Basic Structure according to the attachment? → Yes.

What is Judicial Activism? → Active constitutional interpretation to protect rights, justice and public welfare.

What is Judicial Restraint? → Cautious exercise of judicial power respecting Legislature and Executive spheres.

What is PIL? → Public Interest Litigation.

Under which Articles is PIL generally filed? → Articles 32 and 226.

When did PIL develop substantially according to the source? → Late 1970s and 1980s.

Must a PIL petitioner always be personally affected? → No.

What is Civil Contempt? → Wilful disobedience of court orders or breach of undertaking.

What is Criminal Contempt? → Acts scandalising court or interfering with judicial proceedings or administration of justice.

Which statute governs contempt according to the source? → Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.

Which Act established Gram Nyayalayas? → Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008.

What is their purpose? → Speedy, inexpensive and accessible rural justice.

Is Collegium expressly mentioned in Constitution? → No.

How did it develop? → Through Judges Cases.

Which is the First Judges Case? → S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, 1981.

What was its broad approach? → Greater Executive role.

Which case established Collegium? → Second Judges Case, 1993.

Which case clarified Collegium? → Third Judges Case, 1998.

What is Supreme Court Collegium composition stated in the attachment? → CJI + four senior-most Supreme Court Judges.

Which Amendment created NJAC? → 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014.

Which Act accompanied it? → NJAC Act, 2014.

What was NJAC composition? → CJI, two senior-most Supreme Court Judges, Union Law Minister and two eminent persons.

Which case struck down NJAC? → Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India, 2015.

What is this known as? → Fourth Judges Case.

Which constitutional principle was central? → Judicial Independence as Basic Structure.

What happened after NJAC was struck down? → Collegium System continued.

Which Amendment attempted to curtail certain judicial powers? → 42nd Amendment, 1976.

Which Amendment restored several such powers? → 43rd Amendment, 1977.

Which Amendment reinforced post-Emergency constitutional safeguards? → 44th Amendment, 1978.

Which case evolved Basic Structure Doctrine? → Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973.

Which Article was central to that case? → Article 368.

Which case earlier dealt with Parliament's power over Fundamental Rights? → Golaknath v. State of Punjab, 1967.

Which case held procedure under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable? → Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, 1978.

Which case recognised Right to Speedy Trial? → Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, 1979.

Which case held Judicial Review and limited amending power are Basic Structure features? → Minerva Mills v. Union of India, 1980.

Which case framed workplace sexual-harassment guidelines? → Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan, 1997.

Which case confirmed High Court Judicial Review over Tribunal decisions? → L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997.

Which Amendment introduced 10% EWS reservation? → 103rd Amendment, 2019.

Which case upheld it according to the attachment? → Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India, 2022.

What is the easiest Supreme Court Article memory line? → 124 Court, 129 Record, 131 Original, 136 SLP, 137 Review, 141 Binding Law, 142 Complete Justice, 143 Advisory.
